label: lem:finite-boundary-continuity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:finite-boundary-continuity}
Let $\beta_j\to\beta\in[0,\infty]$, and let
$0<t_*<T<\infty$. Then
\[
 \sup_{t_*\le t\le T}
 \left(
 \|p_{\beta_j}(t)-p_\beta(t)\|_{L^\infty(\overline H)}
 +\|q_{\beta_j}(t)-q_\beta(t)\|_{L^\infty(\overline H)}
 \right)\longrightarrow0.
\]
At $\beta=\infty$, the limiting pair is
$(p_\infty,0)$. At $\beta=0$, the limiting pair
is obtained by folding the homogeneous solution,
and its two interface traces agree.
head: environment
name: Finite-time continuity up to the interface

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathsf T_\kappa(t)$ denote the heat semigroup
on $H$ with Robin coefficient $\kappa$.
We use the endpoint conventions
\[
 \mathsf T_0=\mathsf T_{\mathrm N},
 \qquad
 \mathsf T_\infty=\mathsf T_{\mathrm D}.
\]
The kernel inequalities
$0\le r_\kappa\le r_{\mathrm N}$ imply, uniformly
for $\kappa\in[0,\infty]$,
\[
 \|\mathsf T_\kappa(t)\|_{L^\infty\to L^\infty}\le1,
 \qquad
 \|\mathsf T_\kappa(t)\|_{L^2\to L^\infty}
 \le C_Nt^{-N/4}.
\]
These estimates include evaluation on $y=0$,
using the continuous positive-time representatives.

We first verify operator convergence away from
time zero. For $0<\kappa<\infty$, positivity and
\eqref{eq:robin-positive} give
\begin{align*}
 &\sup_{y\ge0}\int_0^\infty
   |r_\kappa(t,y,z)-r_{\mathrm D}(t,y,z)|\,\mathrm d z\\
 &\qquad=
 \sup_{y\ge0}
 2\int_0^\infty\mathrm e^{-\kappa a}G_t^1(y+a)\,\mathrm d a
 \le\frac{C}{\kappa\sqrt t}.
\end{align*}
Similarly, \eqref{eq:robin} gives
\begin{align*}
 &\sup_{y\ge0}\int_0^\infty
   |r_{\mathrm N}(t,y,z)-r_\kappa(t,y,z)|\,\mathrm d z\\
 &\qquad\le
 2\kappa\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty
       G_t^1(z+a)\,\mathrm d z\,\mathrm d a
 \le C\kappa\sqrt t.
\end{align*}
For a finite positive coefficient $\kappa_*$,
the same formula yields
\[
 \sup_{y\ge0}\int_0^\infty
 |r_\kappa(t,y,z)-r_{\kappa_*}(t,y,z)|\,\mathrm d z
 \le
 \int_0^\infty
 |\kappa\mathrm e^{-\kappa a}
       -\kappa_*\mathrm e^{-\kappa_*a}|\,\mathrm d a,
\]
whose right-hand side tends to zero as
$\kappa\to\kappa_*$.
The tangential heat kernel has mass one.
Consequently, for every $0<h<T$ and every
$\kappa_j\to\kappa_*\in[0,\infty]$,
\[
 \sup_{h\le t\le T}
 \|\mathsf T_{\kappa_j}(t)-\mathsf T_{\kappa_*}(t)
       \|_{L^\infty\to L^\infty}
 \longrightarrow0.
\]
In particular, this convergence is uniform up to
the flat boundary.

Write
\[
 \mathbf U_\beta=(S_\beta,D_\beta),\qquad
 \mathsf S_\beta(t)
 =\operatorname{diag}
   \bigl(\mathsf T_{\mathrm N}(t),
         \mathsf T_{2/\beta}(t)\bigr),
\]
with $2/0=\infty$ and $2/\infty=0$.
The folded reaction vector is
\[
 \mathcal F(S,D)
 =\frac12
 \begin{pmatrix}
 f(S+D)+f(S-D)\\
 f(S+D)-f(S-D)
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
It is bounded and Lipschitz on the common invariant
region $0\le S-D\le S+D\le1$.

Fix $0<h<t_*/2$. For $t\in[t_*,T]$, apply the
mild formula on the short interval $[t-h,t]$:
\[
 \mathbf U_\beta(t)
 =\mathsf S_\beta(h)\mathbf U_\beta(t-h)
 +\int_{t-h}^t
   \mathsf S_\beta(t-s)\mathcal F(\mathbf U_\beta(s))
   \,\mathrm d s.
\]
Subtract the corresponding formula for $\beta_j$.
The two recent-time integrals have total
$L^\infty$ norm at most $Ch$, uniformly in the
parameters. For the initial term, insert and subtract
$\mathsf S_{\beta_j}(h)\mathbf U_\beta(t-h)$.
The smoothing estimate and operator convergence
then give
\begin{align*}
 &\sup_{t_*\le t\le T}
 \|\mathbf U_{\beta_j}(t)-\mathbf U_\beta(t)\|_\infty\\
 &\quad\le
 C h^{-N/4}
 \sup_{0\le s\le T}
 \|\mathbf U_{\beta_j}(s)-\mathbf U_\beta(s)\|_2\\
 &\qquad+
 \|\mathsf S_{\beta_j}(h)-\mathsf S_\beta(h)
       \|_{L^\infty\to L^\infty}
 \sup_{0\le s\le T}\|\mathbf U_\beta(s)\|_\infty
 +Ch.
\end{align*}
The already established $C([0,T];L^2)$ convergence
makes the first term vanish as $j\to\infty$.
For fixed $h$, operator convergence makes the second
term vanish as well. Thus the limit superior is
bounded by $Ch$. Letting $h\downarrow0$ proves
uniform convergence of the folded pair.
Since $p=S+D$ and $q=S-D$, the asserted convergence
of both densities follows, including at $y=0$.

label: lem:envelope
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:envelope}
For every $0<\sigma<1/4$, there exist constants
$C_\sigma,c>0$, independent of $\beta\in[0,\infty]$,
such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:envelope}
 u(t,x)\le
 C_\sigma(z+t^\sigma)\mathrm e^{-z}\mathrm e^{-cz^2/t},
 \qquad z=|x|-m(t)\ge0,\quad t\ge2.
\end{equation}
Both interface traces are included in this estimate.
The same bound holds for the even Neumann extension $P$,
after adjusting the constants.
head: environment
name: A uniform Gaussian envelope

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a compactly supported radial upper datum as above.
The corresponding homogeneous solution dominates every
interface solution, including both traces, independently
of the resistance. Lemma~\ref{lem:linear-envelope} in
Appendix~\ref{app:linear}, together with $f(u)\le u$,
gives \eqref{eq:envelope} for this radial solution and
hence for $u$. Applying the same construction to
a radial datum dominating the initial density of $P$
gives the estimate for $P$.

The construction uses only linear comparison and
the explicit supersolution of Appendix~\ref{app:linear},
independently of the subsequent front-localization
and matching arguments.

head: environment
name: Boundary dissipation

label: eq:cutoff-error
title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi_0$ with $0\le\chi_0\le1$, $\chi_0=0$ on $(-\infty,1]$, and $\chi_0=1$ on $[2,\infty)$. Set
\[
 \chi(\tau,\rho)=\chi_0(\rho/a(t)),\qquad \Psi(X)=(1+|X|^2)^M.
\]
Testing \eqref{eq:W} with $\chi^2\Psi W$, initially with compact outer cutoffs, produces the nonnegative boundary dissipation
\[
 \kappa\sqrt t\int_{Y=0}\chi^2\Psi W^2.
\]
The polynomial weight satisfies
\[
 |\nabla\Psi|^2/\Psi\le C_M\Psi,\qquad |X\cdot\nabla\Psi|\le C_M\Psi.
\]
The potential is controlled by \eqref{eq:V-small}. Moreover, $\partial_\tau\chi$ is uniformly bounded and supported in $a(t)\le\rho\le2a(t)$. The cutoff terms are therefore controlled by the weighted energy and
\[
 Ca(t)^{-2}\int_{a(t)\le\rho\le2a(t),\ Y>0}\Psi W^2\,\mathrm d X.
\]
To estimate this term, write
\[
 l=m(t)+\rho\sqrt t,\qquad r=\sqrt{l^2+t|(v,Y)|^2},\qquad d=r-l\ge0.
\]
Since $0\le D_\beta\le p_\beta/2$, the Gaussian envelope gives
\[
 W\le C\bigl(\rho+d/\sqrt t+t^{\sigma-1/2}\bigr)\mathrm e^{-c\rho^2}\mathrm e^{-d}.
\]
On the cutoff layer, $l$ is comparable to $t$, and
\[
 d=\frac{t|(v,Y)|^2}{r+l}\ge c\frac{|(v,Y)|^2}{1+|(v,Y)|}.
\]
Hence integration against any fixed polynomial weight yields
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R^{N-2}}\int_0^\infty\Psi W^2\,\mathrm d Y\,\mathrm d v
 \le C_M\bigl(a(t)^2+t^{-1}+t^{2\sigma-1}\bigr).
\]
The layer has width $a(t)$, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cutoff-error}
 Ca(t)^{-2}\int_{a(t)\le\rho\le2a(t),\ Y>0}\Psi W^2\,\mathrm d X
 \le C_M\left(a(t)+\frac{t^{-1}}{a(t)}+\frac{t^{2\sigma-1}}{a(t)}\right)\le C_M.
\end{equation}
This proves \eqref{eq:cutoff-error}.

The same envelope gives a uniform bound for
\[
 E(\tau)=\int_{Y>0}\chi^2\Psi W^2\,\mathrm d X.
\]
For large $\rho$, the estimate
\[
 d\ge c\frac{|(v,Y)|^2}{1+\rho+|(v,Y)|}
\]
combined with $\mathrm e^{-c\rho^2}$ controls all polynomial moments and justifies removing the outer cutoffs. After absorbing the gradient cross terms, the energy inequality therefore gives
\[
 E'(\tau)+\kappa\sqrt t\int_{Y=0}\chi^2\Psi W^2\le C_M(E(\tau)+1).
\]
Integrating over $[\log T,\log(2T)]$, whose length is $\log2$, and using the uniform bound on $E$, we obtain
\[
 \int_{\log T}^{\log(2T)}\kappa\sqrt t\int_{Y=0}\chi^2\Psi W^2\,\mathrm d\tau\le C_M.
\]
Since $\kappa\ge2/B$, $t\ge T$, and $\chi=1$ for $\rho\ge2a(t)$, this proves \eqref{eq:trace-energy}.

Finally, $W\ge0$, and the condition $M>(N+1)/2$ ensures
\[
 \int_0^\infty\int_{\mathbb R^{N-2}}\frac{(1+\rho)^2}{(1+\rho^2+|v|^2)^M}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d\rho<\infty.
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz in space and logarithmic time now gives \eqref{eq:trace-L1}.

label: lem:robin-local
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:robin-local}
Let $X_0\in\{Y=0\}$ and $0<r<R\le1$. Define
\[
 B_R^+=B_R(X_0)\cap\{Y>0\},\qquad
 Q_R^+=(s_0-R^2,s_0]\times B_R^+,
\]
and
\[
 \Gamma_R=(s_0-R^2,s_0]\times(B_R(X_0)\cap\{Y=0\}).
\]
Suppose that $w\ge0$ is a subsolution of
\[
 w_s\le\Delta w+b\cdot\nabla w+cw\quad\text{in }Q_R^+,
 \qquad \partial_nw+\lambda w\le0\quad\text{on }\Gamma_R,
\]
where $n=-e_Y$, $|b|+c_+\le M$, and $\lambda\ge0$. The boundary coefficient $\lambda$ may depend on space and time and is locally bounded for each subsolution; no uniform upper bound on $\lambda$ is assumed. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:robin-local-sup}
 \|w\|_{L^\infty(Q_r^+)}
 \le\frac{C(N,M)}{(R-r)^{(N+2)/2}}\|w\|_{L^2(Q_R^+)}.
\end{equation}
The constant is independent of $\lambda$. If $w$ is continuous up to the flat boundary, the same bound holds on $\Gamma_r$. The conclusion also holds when the Robin inequality is replaced by homogeneous Dirichlet data on the flat boundary.
head: environment
name: Local estimate independent of the Robin coefficient

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a space--time cutoff $0\le\zeta\le1$, equal to one on $Q_r^+$, vanishing at the initial time and near the curved spatial boundary of $Q_R^+$, and satisfying
\[
 |\nabla\zeta|\le\frac{C}{R-r},\qquad
 |\partial_s\zeta|\le\frac{C}{(R-r)^2}.
\]
The cutoff may be nonzero on the flat boundary.

For $p\ge2$, test the differential inequality with $\zeta^2w^{p-1}$. The boundary condition gives
\[
 \int_{\{Y=0\}}\zeta^2w^{p-1}\partial_nw
 \le-\int_{\{Y=0\}}\lambda\zeta^2w^p.
\]
Thus the Robin term contributes nonnegative dissipation after it is moved to the left-hand side. Estimate the drift directly by Young's inequality, without differentiating $b$, and use $c\le c_+\le M$. Setting $v=w^{p/2}$, integrating in time, and taking the supremum of the spatial energy yields
\begin{align}\label{eq:robin-local-energy}
 &\sup_s\int_{B_R^+}\zeta^2v^2
 +\int_{Q_R^+}|\nabla(\zeta v)|^2
 +p\int_{\Gamma_R}\lambda\zeta^2v^2\notag\\
 &\qquad\le Cp^2\int_{Q_R^+}
 \bigl(|\partial_s\zeta|+|\nabla\zeta|^2+(1+M^2)\zeta^2\bigr)v^2.
\end{align}
No upper bound or derivative bound on $\lambda$ enters this estimate. Truncated and regularized power tests justify the calculation for weak subsolutions. Under homogeneous Dirichlet conditions, the boundary contribution vanishes.

Extend $\zeta v$ evenly across $\{Y=0\}$. Since it vanishes near the curved boundary, the extension belongs to $H_0^1(B_R(X_0))$. The parabolic Sobolev inequality therefore applies with a constant depending only on $N$; only the test function is extended, not the equation. With $\chi=1+2/N$, the energy estimate \eqref{eq:robin-local-energy} gives
\[
 \|w\|_{L^{p\chi}(Q_r^+)}
 \le\left[\frac{C(N,M)p^2}{(R-r)^2}\right]^{1/p}\|w\|_{L^p(Q_R^+)}.
\]
Here $R-r\le1$ allows the zeroth-order contribution to be included in the same factor.

Iterate this inequality with
\[
 p_j=2\chi^j,\qquad R_j=r+(R-r)2^{-j},\qquad j=0,1,\ldots,
\]
using $R_j$ as the outer radius and $R_{j+1}$ as the inner radius. Since
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^\infty\frac{2}{p_j}=\frac{N+2}{2},\qquad
 \sum_{j=0}^\infty\frac{j+\log p_j}{p_j}<\infty,
\]
the iteration yields \eqref{eq:robin-local-sup}. Continuity up to the flat boundary gives the trace estimate.

label: prop:moment
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:moment}
For every $0<B<\infty$, there exists a limiting moment $E_\beta^\infty(\theta)$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Etail}
 |E_\beta(t,\theta)-E_\beta^\infty(\theta)|\le C_Bt^{-1/4}.
\end{equation}
for all sufficiently large $t$, uniformly for $0\le\beta\le B$ and $\theta\in\overline{\mathbb S_+}$. The limit is jointly continuous in $(\beta,\theta)$ on $[0,B]\times\overline{\mathbb S_+}$.

At equatorial directions, the stronger estimate
\[
 |E_\beta(t,(\eta,0))-E_\beta^\infty(\eta,0)|\le Ct^{-\mu}(1+\log t),\qquad \mu=\frac12-2\sigma=\frac38,
\]
holds uniformly for $\eta\in\mathbb S^{N-2}$ and $\beta\in[0,\infty]$.
head: environment
name: Uniform moment convergence on the closed receiving hemisphere

title: Proof
body_md:
The volume contribution is controlled by \eqref{eq:absorption-tail}. It remains to estimate the interface contribution in \eqref{eq:moment-balance} uniformly as the direction approaches the equator.

On each fixed receiving cone, use $D\le p_\infty/2$ and the linear Neumann Gaussian upper bound; the tilted interface term is exponentially integrable. Near the equator write $\theta=(b\eta,s)$, $b=\sqrt{1-s^2}\ge1/2$, and $\lambda=1-b$. For $s>0$, the change of variables \eqref{eq:cartesian} bounds the absolute interface contribution by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Itau}
 2s t^{-1+k\lambda}\mathrm e^{-2\lambda t}
 \int_{\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{N-2}} |1-2\lambda t-bk\log t+b\rho\sqrt t|
       \mathrm e^{-\lambda\rho\sqrt t}W(\tau,\rho,v,0)\,\mathrm d\rho\,\mathrm d v.
\end{equation}
On $\rho\ge2a(t)$, maximizing the scalar coefficients over $s$ and using $s^2=\lambda(1+b)$ bounds \eqref{eq:Itau} by
\[
 Ct^{-1}\int_{\rho\ge2a(t)}(1+\rho)W(\tau,\rho,v,0)\,\mathrm d\rho\,\mathrm d v.
\]
The factor $t^{k\lambda}$ is absorbed into $\mathrm e^{-\lambda t}$ for large $t$. Integration over $t\in[T,2T]$, using $\,\mathrm d t/t=\,\mathrm d\tau$ and \eqref{eq:trace-L1}, gives $C_BT^{-1/4}$.

For the complementary part $l=\eta\cdot x'\le m+2t^\gamma$, first restrict to $r'=|x'|\le m+4t^\gamma$. Near the front, tangential angular integration contributes $t^{(N-2)/2}$, so the tilted radial factor is $t^{-2+k\lambda}\mathrm e^{-2\lambda t}$. For $r'=m+z$, $0\le z\le4t^\gamma$, the remaining integral is bounded by
\[
 C\int_0^{4t^\gamma}(z+t^\sigma)(1+\lambda t+\log t+z)\,\mathrm d z.
\]
Multiplication by $s$ and maximization give
$Ct^{-5/2+3\gamma}(1+\log t)$. The part $z<0$ is smaller, using $u\le1$. If $r'>m+4t^\gamma$ but $l\le m+2t^\gamma$, then $r'-l\ge2t^\gamma$; the factor $\mathrm e^{-b(r'-l)}$ makes this remainder superpolynomially small. Since $\gamma=1/4$, the complementary contribution integrated over $[T,2T]$ is $O(T^{-3/4}\log T)$.

Summing the dyadic bounds and the volume tail with $\sigma=1/16$ proves \eqref{eq:Etail}. At each fixed positive time, parameter continuity and the common Gaussian bound make $E_\beta(t,\theta)$ jointly continuous. Uniform convergence therefore gives joint continuity of the limit. At $s=0$, the interface contribution vanishes identically, and integration of \eqref{eq:absorption-tail} gives the stronger equatorial estimate.

label: lem:wave-tails
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Wave tails and derivative ratios

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $w=1-U_*$, $a=-f'(1)>0$ and $\lambda=\lambda_*$.
Then $w'>0$, $\lambda^2+2\lambda=a$, and
\[
 w''+2w'=f(1-w)=aw+R(w),\qquad R(w)=O(w^2).
\]
First, $v=w'$ is bounded. Indeed, $v'+2v=f(1-w)\ge0$
implies $v(r)\ge\mathrm e^{-2(r-s)}v(s)$ for $r\ge s$, whereas
$\int_s^{s+1}v(r)\,\mathrm d r\le1$; hence
$v(s)\le2/(1-\mathrm e^{-2})$. Thus $q=w'-\lambda w$ is bounded
and satisfies $q'+(\lambda+2)q=R(w)$. Variation of constants
from $-\infty$ gives, for all sufficiently negative $s$,
\[
 q(s)=\int_{-\infty}^s\mathrm e^{-(\lambda+2)(s-r)}R(w(r))\,\mathrm d r
      =O(w(s)^2),
\]
where we used monotonicity of $w$. Consequently,
$(\log w)'=\lambda+O(w)\ge\lambda/2$ on a left half-line.
Integrating backwards gives $w(s)\le C\mathrm e^{\lambda s/2}$,
so $w$ is integrable at $-\infty$. Since
\[
 \frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm d s}\log(w(s)\mathrm e^{-\lambda s})=O(w(s)),
\]
this logarithm has a finite real limit there. Thus
$w(s)\sim B_-\mathrm e^{\lambda s}$ with $B_->0$.
Integrating the last identity once more yields
$w=B_-\mathrm e^{\lambda s}+O(\mathrm e^{2\lambda s})$.
The identity $w'=\lambda w+q$ and the wave equation give
the asserted first and second derivative expansions.

For the right tail set $V(s)=\mathrm e^sU_*(s)$. The normalization
in \eqref{eq:wave} gives $V(s)/s\to1$, while
\[
 V''(s)=\mathrm e^s g(U_*(s))\ge0,\qquad
 V''(s)=O((1+s)^2\mathrm e^{-s}).
\]
The second estimate makes $V''$ integrable at $+\infty$;
the limiting value of $V'$ must be $1$, since $V(s)/s\to1$.
Therefore
\[
 V'(s)-1=-\int_s^\infty V''(r)\,\mathrm d r
       =O((1+s)^2\mathrm e^{-s}).
\]
This error is also integrable, so $V(s)-s$ has a finite
limit $B_+$ and
$V(s)=s+B_++O((1+s)^2\mathrm e^{-s})$.
Using $U_*'=\mathrm e^{-s}(V'-V)$ and
$U_*''=\mathrm e^{-s}(V''-2V'+V)$ proves the three right-tail
expansions without differentiating an uncontrolled remainder.
Division yields \eqref{eq:wave-ratio} at both ends.
On compact intervals, continuity and $U_*'<0$ bound $r_U$.

label: lem:coarse
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:coarse}
Fix $0<B<\infty$, $0<\gamma<1/3$, and $\gamma<\delta<1/2$. In the moving Cartesian coordinates
\[
 x=(m(t)+z)\theta+\zeta,\qquad
 \zeta\perp\theta,\qquad |\zeta|\le t^\delta,
\]
define
\[
 h(t,z,\theta,\zeta)=z-U_*^{-1}(u(t,x)).
\]
On each fixed receiving cone $\Gamma_{\delta_0}$, $0<\delta_0\le1$, the following estimates hold for all sufficiently large $t$, uniformly for $0\le\beta\le B$, $\theta\in\Gamma_{\delta_0}$, and the indicated transverse displacements:
\begin{align}
 |h|&\le C,&&0\le z\le t^\gamma,\label{eq:h-ahead}\\
 |h|&\le C_\epsilon+\epsilon|z|,&&-Z\le z\le0,\label{eq:h-behind}
\end{align}
for every $\epsilon>0$ and $Z>0$ in the second estimate. The same bounds hold in equatorial coordinates for each folded component. In \eqref{eq:h-behind}, $C_\epsilon$ is independent of $Z$, although the starting time may depend on $Z$.
head: environment
name: Coarse displacement bounds

label: eq:sharp-upper
title: Proof
body_md:
We derive the bounds from scalar comparisons, independently of the multidimensional wave convergence to be proved below.

First, the radial linear supersolution gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sharp-upper}
 u(t,x)\le C(1+z_r)\mathrm e^{-z_r},\qquad
 0\le z_r:=|x|-m(t)\le2t^\gamma.
\end{equation}
Indeed, apply Lemma~\ref{lem:linear-envelope} in Appendix~\ref{app:linear} with $\sigma=0$. Then $\eta_t=t^{-1/2}$, the inner boundary is $z_r=-1$, and the coefficient bounds give bounded $\zeta_{\rm lin}$ and $Q\asymp\eta_t$. Here $\zeta_{\rm lin}$ is the scalar coefficient in \eqref{eq:linear-Phi}. The comparison accommodates both the inner-boundary data and the Gaussian tail at the starting time. The normalized supersolution is therefore bounded by $C(\rho+\eta_t)$ for $0\le\rho\le1$, which yields \eqref{eq:sharp-upper} after multiplication by $\sqrt t\,\mathrm e^{-z_r}$. This construction uses only $f(u)\le u$.

For the lower bound, use the common radial seed and the inequality $f(u)\ge u-C_fu^2$. The auxiliary logistic matching estimate in Appendix~\ref{app:logistic} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sharp-lower}
 u(t,x)\ge c(1+z_r)\mathrm e^{-z_r},\qquad 0\le z_r\le2t^\gamma.
\end{equation}
Its weighted matching error is $O(t^{3\gamma-1})$, which tends to zero because $\gamma<1/3$. The fixed time shift used to insert the seed changes only the constants.

Since
\[
 z_r-z=\frac{|\zeta|^2}{|x|+m(t)+z}=O(t^{2\delta-1}),
\]
the bounds \eqref{eq:sharp-upper}--\eqref{eq:sharp-lower}, together with the right-hand wave tail, imply \eqref{eq:h-ahead} for sufficiently large positive $z$. It remains to control bounded values of $z$ and the region behind the front.

For this purpose, consider the common radial comparison solutions with the original reaction $f$. Their leading-edge identification and relative mesoscopic matching use only $g\ge0$ and the radial envelope. On $|z_r|\le t^\gamma$, the radial moving-frame equation has drift
\[
 2+b(t,z_r),\qquad
 b(t,z_r)=-\frac{k}{t}+\frac{N-1}{m(t)+z_r},\qquad |b(t,z_r)|\le C/t.
\]
Let $\mathcal U(t,z)$ denote one of the radial
comparison solutions in its moving coordinate
$z=r-m(t)$, and let $a>0$ be its leading-edge
amplitude. Fix $0<\varepsilon<a$ and put
$R(t)=t^\gamma$.
The relative mesoscopic estimate allows us to
choose $T_\varepsilon$ sufficiently large that,
for every $t\ge T_\varepsilon$,
\[
 (a-\varepsilon)R(t)\mathrm e^{-R(t)}
 \le \mathcal U(t,R(t))
 \le (a+\varepsilon)R(t)\mathrm e^{-R(t)}.
\]
Increase $T_\varepsilon$ if necessary so that
the prescribed right boundary values lie in $[0,1]$
and $m(t)-R(t)>0$.

On $-R(t)<z<R(t)$, let $q_-$ and $q_+$ solve
\[
 (q_\pm)_t
 =(q_\pm)_{zz}+(2+b(t,z))(q_\pm)_z+f(q_\pm),
\]
with boundary values
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 q_-(t,-R(t))&=0,
 &q_-(t,R(t))&=(a-\varepsilon)R(t)\mathrm e^{-R(t)},\\
 q_+(t,-R(t))&=1,
 &q_+(t,R(t))&=(a+\varepsilon)R(t)\mathrm e^{-R(t)},
 \end{aligned}
\]
and initial profiles
\[
 q_-(T_\varepsilon,z)=0,\qquad
 q_+(T_\varepsilon,z)=1
 \quad(-R(T_\varepsilon)<z<R(T_\varepsilon)).
\]
The initial profiles need not agree with the
boundary data at the two initial corners;
this is permitted in Lemma~\ref{lem:energy}.
Comparison with the constants $0$ and $1$ gives
$0\le q_\pm\le1$.
The initial and lateral inequalities then yield
\[
 q_-(t,z)\le\mathcal U(t,z)\le q_+(t,z),
 \qquad t>T_\varepsilon,\quad |z|<R(t).
\]

Lemma~\ref{lem:energy}, whose argument is adapted
from \cite[Lemma 4.1]{Wang}, applies because
$|b(t,z)|\le C/t$.
In particular, the drift contribution
\[
 \int V_t\,b(V_z-V)
\]
is estimated by Young's inequality without
differentiating $b$. The resulting errors
\[
 Ct^{2\gamma-2}(\mathcal F+C)+Ct^{3\gamma-2}
\]
are integrable since $\gamma<1/3$.
Thus, for each fixed $\varepsilon$,
\[
 q_\pm(t,z)\longrightarrow
 U_*\bigl(z-\log(a\pm\varepsilon)\bigr)
\]
locally uniformly in $z$ as $t\to\infty$.
The comparison consequently gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 U_*\bigl(z-\log(a-\varepsilon)\bigr)
 &\le\liminf_{t\to\infty}\mathcal U(t,z)\\
 &\le\limsup_{t\to\infty}\mathcal U(t,z)
 \le U_*\bigl(z-\log(a+\varepsilon)\bigr).
 \end{aligned}
\]
First let $t\to\infty$ with $\varepsilon$ fixed,
and then let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$.
Continuity of the translated wave, uniformly on
compact $z$-intervals, proves
\[
 \mathcal U(t,z)\longrightarrow U_*(z-\log a)
\]
locally uniformly in $z$.

The radial comparison solutions are nonincreasing in radius. Their convergence bounds $u$ away from both $0$ and $1$ on each fixed interval of $z_r$, completing \eqref{eq:h-ahead}. It also gives uniform saturation behind the front.

To quantify the latter statement, fix a sufficiently small $0<\varepsilon<\lambda_*$. We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:negative-tail}
 c_\varepsilon\mathrm e^{(\lambda_*+\varepsilon)z_r}
 \le1-u(t,x)\le C_\varepsilon\mathrm e^{(\lambda_*-\varepsilon)z_r}
\end{equation}
for sufficiently large $t$ in the region
\[
 t\le|x|\le m(t)-Z_0,
\]
where $Z_0$ is chosen sufficiently large. The constants do not depend on a subsequent fixed left cutoff in the moving coordinate.

Set $v=1-u$ and $\omega_*=-f'(1)>0$. Then
\[
 v_t=\Delta v+A(t,x)v,
\]
and saturation makes $|A+\omega_*|$ arbitrarily small in $|x|\le m(t)-Z_0$. Put $\nu_\pm=\lambda_*\pm\varepsilon$. Upper and lower comparison functions on this ball are, respectively,
\[
 C\exp\!\left[
 \nu_-\bigl(\sqrt{|x|^2+R_0^2}-m(t)\bigr)
 \right],\qquad
 c\,\mathrm e^{-\nu_+m(t)}\cosh(\nu_+|x|).
\]
Choose $R_0$ large, then make the coefficient error small by increasing $Z_0$, and finally take the starting time large. The differential inequalities follow from
\[
 \omega_*-2\nu_- -\nu_-^2>0,\qquad
 \omega_*-2\nu_+ -\nu_+^2<0,
\]
together with
\[
 |\nabla\sqrt{|x|^2+R_0^2}|\le1,\qquad
 \Delta\sqrt{|x|^2+R_0^2}\le N/R_0,
\]
and
\[
 \Delta\cosh(\nu_+|x|)\ge\nu_+^2\cosh(\nu_+|x|).
\]
The scalar radial comparisons provide the required bounds at the moving outer boundary. The constants $c,C$ can be chosen to fit the data on the finite starting ball, and both radial comparison functions satisfy every transmission condition. On $|x|\ge t$, these bounds give \eqref{eq:negative-tail}.

Finally, the left-hand wave asymptotics convert \eqref{eq:negative-tail} into a bound of the form
\[
 |h|\le C_\varepsilon+C\varepsilon|z|.
\]
Combining this with the bounded-interval estimates and choosing the auxiliary $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small proves \eqref{eq:h-behind}. For each fixed $Z$, the corresponding points satisfy $|x|\ge t$ once $t$ is sufficiently large, which explains the allowed dependence of the starting time on $Z$.

label: lem:localization
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Uniform front localization

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $U$ be the common radial upper solution, and let
$w(t-t_0,\cdot)$ be the common radial lower solution
inserted at time $t_0$, as constructed in
Section~\ref{sec:prelim}. Thus
\[
 w(t-t_0,x)\le u(t,x)\le U(t,x),
 \qquad t\ge t_0,\quad 0\le\beta\le B.
\]
Both comparison solutions are nonincreasing in radius.

The radial wave convergence established in the
proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:coarse} gives finite constants
$\xi_-$ and $\xi_+$ such that, locally uniformly in $z$,
\[
 w(t-t_0,m(t)+z)\longrightarrow U_*(z-\xi_-),
 \qquad
 U(t,m(t)+z)\longrightarrow U_*(z-\xi_+).
\]
Here the radial solutions are written as functions of
radius, and the fixed time shift is absorbed into $\xi_-$,
using $m(t)-m(t-t_0)\to2t_0$.

For each fixed $A>0$, radial monotonicity gives
\[
 \inf_{\substack{0\le\beta\le B\\|x|\le m(t)-A}}
 u^\beta(t,x)\ge w(t-t_0,m(t)-A),
\]
and
\[
 \sup_{\substack{0\le\beta\le B\\|x|\ge m(t)+A}}
 u^\beta(t,x)\le U(t,m(t)+A).
\]
First let $t\to\infty$, and then let $A\to\infty$.
The limits $U_*(-\infty)=1$ and $U_*(+\infty)=0$
prove both assertions.
head: environment

label: lem:common-comparison
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:common-comparison}
Let $I=[s_0,s_1]$ be a finite time interval and set
\[
 \mathcal B=(-Z,\ell)\times(-R,R)^{N-2}\times(0,R).
\]
Let $\Gamma$ denote the relative interior of its face $y=0$.
Suppose two subsolutions are $C^{1,2}$ in the interior,
continuous on the closed cylinder, and have continuous
one-sided normal derivatives on the relative interior of
$\Gamma$ at positive times. Suppose they satisfy
\begin{align*}
 (\partial_s-\Delta-d_i\partial_z-c_i)v_i&\le0
       &&\text{in }I\times\mathcal B,\\
 \partial_nv_i+a_i(v_i-v_{3-i})&\le0
       &&\text{on }I\times\Gamma,
\end{align*}
where $d_i,c_i$ are bounded and $a_i\ge0$ are continuous
on the closed exchange face. All coefficients may depend
on time and position, and $a_1=a_2$ is not required.

Suppose a common scalar function $B$ satisfies
\[
 (\partial_s-\Delta-d_i\partial_z-c_i)B\ge0
 \quad(i=1,2),\qquad
 \partial_nB\ge0\quad\text{on }I\times\Gamma.
\]
If $v_i\le B$ initially and on all other spatial faces,
including their edges by continuity, then $v_i\le B$
throughout the cylinder. The conclusion requires no
quantitative upper bound on $a_i$. In particular, common
barriers give uniform estimates for families whose exchange
coefficients are not uniformly bounded.
head: environment
name: A common supersolution for boundary exchange

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $w_i=v_i-B$. Since the same function $B$ is subtracted
from both components,
\[
 (\partial_s-\Delta-d_i\partial_z-c_i)w_i\le0,\qquad
 \partial_nw_i+a_i(w_i-w_{3-i})\le0.
\]
Multiply by $\mathrm e^{-C_0(s-s_0)}$, where
$C_0>\max_i\sup c_i$, and relabel the resulting functions
as $w_i$. Their zeroth-order coefficients are now
$\widetilde c_i=c_i-C_0<0$, while their exchange conditions
are unchanged.

To obtain strict inequalities, subtract from both components
$\delta\psi$, where
\[
 \psi(s,y)=\mathrm e^{K_0(s-s_0)}[1+(R-y)^2],
 \qquad \delta>0.
\]
Choose $K_0$ large enough that
\[
 (\partial_s-\Delta-d_i\partial_z-\widetilde c_i)\psi>0
 \quad(i=1,2).
\]
This choice uses only the interior coefficient bounds and
the finite box. Moreover,
\[
 \partial_n\psi=2R\mathrm e^{K_0(s-s_0)}>0
 \qquad(y=0).
\]
The functions $\widetilde w_i=w_i-\delta\psi$ therefore
satisfy strict interior and exchange inequalities; the common
perturbation cancels from the exchange differences.

A positive maximum over both components and the closed
space-time cylinder cannot occur initially or on a prescribed
spatial face. An interior maximum contradicts the strict
parabolic inequality and $\widetilde c_i<0$. At a maximum
on $\Gamma$, the maximizing component satisfies
\[
 \widetilde w_i\ge\widetilde w_{3-i},
 \qquad \partial_n\widetilde w_i\ge0.
\]
Since $a_i\ge0$, this gives
\[
 \partial_n\widetilde w_i
   +a_i(\widetilde w_i-\widetilde w_{3-i})\ge0,
\]
contrary to the strict exchange inequality. Edges are covered
by the prescribed-face inequalities and continuity.
Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ proves the assertion. No derivative
or quantitative upper bound of $a_i$ enters the argument.
head: environment

label: lem:persistence
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Persistence of a positive seed

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $t_0>0$ be a time at which the seed is dominated. Since $Q$ is bounded, heat comparison gives, at every fixed $T>t_0$,
\[
 V(T,x)\ge c_T
 \exp\left(-\frac{(|x|+M_0)^2}{4(T-t_0)}\right),
\]
where $M_0$ bounds the support radius of the seed and $c_T>0$.

Use logarithmic time $\tau=\log t$ and, in the exterior region, set
\[
 \rho=\frac{|x|-m(t)}{\sqrt t},\qquad
 \eta_t=t^{\sigma-1/2},\qquad
 X=\rho-\eta_t>0,
\]
\[
 c_t=\frac14+\eta_t,\qquad
 F(\tau,\rho)=X\mathrm e^{-c_tX^2}.
\]
For the coefficients in \eqref{eq:coefficients}, direct differentiation yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gaussian-residual}
 \frac{(\partial_\tau-L_0-p_{\rm rad}\partial_\rho)F}{F}
 =6\eta_t
 -\bigl[(1/2+\sigma)\eta_t+4\eta_t^2\bigr]X^2
 -(\sigma\eta_t+p_{\rm rad})(X^{-1}-2c_tX).
\end{equation}
Here
\[
 r=m(t)+\rho\sqrt t>m(t)+t^\sigma>2t
\]
for sufficiently large $t$. Consequently,
\[
 q_c\ge0,\qquad
 -\frac{k}{\sqrt t}\le p_{\rm rad}<0,\qquad
 \sigma\eta_t+p_{\rm rad}>0.
\]
The singular term $-(\sigma\eta_t+p_{\rm rad})X^{-1}$ is nonpositive. The remaining positive linear term in $X$ is bounded by $C\eta_tX$ and can be absorbed into the negative quadratic term, leaving an upper bound $C\eta_t$ for the residual in \eqref{eq:gaussian-residual}.

The assumed envelope bound also gives
\[
 tQ(t,x)\le Ct^{1+\sigma}\mathrm e^{-t^\sigma}
 \qquad\bigl(|x|\ge m(t)+t^\sigma\bigr).
\]
Both error bounds are integrable in logarithmic time. Define
\[
 \chi(\tau)=\chi(\log T)
 \exp\left[
 -\int_{\log T}^{\tau}
 \left(
 C\mathrm e^{(\sigma-1/2)s}
 +C\mathrm e^{(1+\sigma)s}\mathrm e^{-\mathrm e^{\sigma s}}
 \right)\,\mathrm d s
 \right].
\]
Then $\chi(\infty)>0$ whenever $\chi(\log T)>0$. The residual estimate and $q_c\ge0$ show that
\[
 \underline V(t,x)
 =\sqrt t\,\mathrm e^{-\rho\sqrt t}\chi(\log t)F(\log t,\rho)
\]
is a radial subsolution of $\partial_t-\Delta-(1-Q)$ in $|x|>m(t)+t^\sigma$. This comparison is valid even when $Q$ is not radial, since its bound is pointwise. The subsolution vanishes on the moving inner boundary.

Choose $T$ sufficiently large that
\[
 \frac14+\eta_T>\frac{T}{4(T-t_0)}.
\]
At time $T$, the subsolution therefore has faster Gaussian decay than the heat lower bound. A sufficiently small $\chi(\log T)>0$ makes $\underline V(T,\cdot)\le V(T,\cdot)$ on the entire exterior region. Exterior comparison gives $\underline V\le V$ for all later times.

Finally, $\eta_t\to0$, $c_t\to1/4$, and $\chi(\log t)\to\chi(\infty)>0$. Hence
\[
 \chi(\log t)F(\log t,\rho)
 \longrightarrow
 \chi(\infty)\rho\mathrm e^{-\rho^2/4}
\]
uniformly on each compact subset of $(0,\infty)$. This proves \eqref{eq:persistence}.

label: lem:Rseed
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Rseed}
Under \eqref{ass:K} and \eqref{ass:C}, the function $R$ in \eqref{eq:coop} is nonzero at some positive time and is strictly positive throughout $\overline H$ at every sufficiently large time.
head: environment
name: Creation of an average-mode seed

title: Proof
body_md:
The function $f'$ is nonincreasing and cannot be constant: otherwise $f'(0)=1$ would contradict $f(1)=f(0)=0$. Since $f\in C^2([0,1])$, there is an $s_*\in(0,1)$ and a neighborhood of $s_*$ on which $f''<0$.

By local convergence to $1$, for some sufficiently large $t_*$ the donor density $p_1(t_*,\cdot)$ exceeds $s_*$ at an interior point. At spatial infinity it tends to zero by the finite-time Gaussian bound. Continuity along a path in $H$ therefore gives an interior point $x_*$ such that
\[
 p_1(t_*,x_*)=s_*.
\]
Since $D_1>0$ in $H$, we have $q_1(t_*,x_*)<s_*$. Concavity and strict decrease of $f'$ immediately below $s_*$ imply
\[
 f'(p_1(t_*,x_*))<f'(q_1(t_*,x_*)).
\]
Thus the integrand defining $B$ is strictly positive at the interpolation endpoint $s=1$. By continuity, $B>0$ on a space-time neighborhood of $(t_*,x_*)$.

Since $Z>0$, the source $BZ$ in the first equation of \eqref{eq:coop} is positive on that neighborhood. Choose $C_0$ such that $A+C_0\ge0$. Then
\[
 R_t-\Delta R+C_0R\ge BZ,
 \qquad \partial_nR=0.
\]
Positivity of the Neumann heat kernel makes $R$ strictly positive throughout $\overline H$ at every time after this positive source has acted. The same argument applies when $\beta_1=0$, since $D_0>0$ in the interior.

label: prop:finite
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:finite}
For every finite $T>0$, there is a constant $C_T$ such
that, uniformly for $0\le t\le T$ as
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-linear}
 \|p_\infty-p_\beta\|_\infty+\|q_\beta\|_\infty
 \le C_T\varepsilon,\qquad
 \|q_\beta/\varepsilon-v\|_\infty\le C_T\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
The norms are taken over $H$, with the boundary traces
included at positive times.

Moreover, on each fixed receiving cone, the exponentially
weighted input moments of $s_\varepsilon$ converge to
those of $p_\infty$. This convergence remains valid after
multiplication by any fixed polynomial weight in time
and tangential position.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The boundary flux
\[
 j=\varepsilon s_\varepsilon
\]
satisfies $0\le j\le\varepsilon$. The Neumann heat
boundary-response operator has $L^\infty$ norm bounded
by $C(t-s)^{-1/2}$: the tangential heat kernel has mass
one, and the normal boundary kernel contributes this
factor.

Set $d=p_\infty-p_\beta$. The mild equations for $d$
and $q_\beta$, together with the Lipschitz continuity of
$f$ on $[0,1]$, yield
\[
 \|d(t)\|_\infty+\|q_\beta(t)\|_\infty
 \le C\varepsilon\sqrt t
 +C\int_0^t
   \bigl(\|d(s)\|_\infty+\|q_\beta(s)\|_\infty\bigr)\,\mathrm d s.
\]
Gronwall's inequality proves the first estimate in
\eqref{eq:finite-linear}.

For the second estimate, put
$w=q_\beta/\varepsilon-v$. Then
\[
 w_t=\Delta w+w-\frac{g(q_\beta)}{\varepsilon},
 \qquad
 \partial_nw=s_\varepsilon-p_\infty,
 \qquad w(0)=0.
\]
The first estimate gives
\[
 \|s_\varepsilon-p_\infty\|_\infty=O_T(\varepsilon).
\]
Since $g(q)\le C_fq^2$, it also gives
\[
 \left\|\frac{g(q_\beta)}{\varepsilon}\right\|_\infty
 =O_T(\varepsilon).
\]
The same heat-kernel estimates therefore imply
$\|w\|_\infty\le C_T\varepsilon$.

For the input moments, use
$0\le s_\varepsilon\le p_\infty$ and the compact-data
linear Neumann upper bound for $p_\infty$.
Tangential exponential tilting produces the factor
\[
 \mathrm e^{-2t}\mathrm e^t\mathrm e^{|\theta'|^2t}
 =\mathrm e^{-\theta_N^2t}.
\]
Thus, for each fixed integer $j\ge0$, the weighted
boundary integral is bounded by a constant times
\[
 t^{-1/2}(1+t)^j
 \mathrm e^{-\delta^2t}\mathrm e^{-d_0^2/(4t)},
\]
where $d_0>0$ is the distance of the initial support
from the interface. This bound is integrable at both
zero and infinity.

Finite-time convergence, followed by dominated convergence,
proves convergence of the weighted input moments.
The domination is uniform for $\theta\in\Gamma_\delta$,
so the convergence is uniform on that cone. This argument
does not assert an $O(\varepsilon)$ rate after integration
over the entire time interval.
head: environment

label: lem:logistic-seed
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Small-seed lower estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $U_\varepsilon$ be the corresponding solution. Fix $0<\zeta<1$, put $L=\log(1/\varepsilon)$, and choose
\[
 A=(1-\zeta)L,\qquad T=L^4.
\]
Suppose $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset B_{R_0}$ and take $\varepsilon$
sufficiently small that $\varepsilon\|\varphi\|_\infty\le1$.
For each $\theta\in\mathbb S^{N-1}$, introduce the moving half-space
\[
 D_t=\{x:\theta\cdot x>2t-A\},\qquad 0\le t\le T.
\]
We construct a linear Dirichlet lower solution in $D_t$ and
compute its kernel explicitly. All constants below may depend
on $\varphi,N,\zeta$, but are independent of $\theta$ and
sufficiently small $\varepsilon$.

Linear comparison gives $U_\varepsilon(t,x)\le C\varepsilon\mathrm e^t$.
For $t\ge A/2\ge1$ and $x\in D_t$, the compact-data heat bound gives
\[
 U_\varepsilon(t,x)
 \le C\varepsilon t^{-N/2}
 \exp\left(t-\frac{[(2t-A-R_0)_+]^2}{4t}\right)
 \le C\varepsilon\mathrm e^{A+R_0}
 \le C\varepsilon^\zeta.
\]
Indeed, with $B=A+R_0$, the exponent is at most $B$:
if $2t\le B$ it equals $t\le B/2$, and otherwise it equals
$B-B^2/(4t)$. Choose a common constant $C$ so that
\[
 q_\varepsilon(t)=
 \begin{cases}
 C\varepsilon\mathrm e^t,&0\le t\le A/2,\\
 C\varepsilon^\zeta,&A/2<t\le T
 \end{cases}
\]
bounds $U_\varepsilon$ throughout $D_t$, and set
$\Lambda_\varepsilon(t)=\int_0^t q_\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm d s$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:seed-absorption-loss}
 0\le \Lambda_\varepsilon(T)
 \le C\left[\varepsilon^{(1+\zeta)/2}
                 +T\varepsilon^\zeta\right]=o(1).
\end{equation}

Let $v$ solve the linear problem
\[
 \begin{cases}
 v_t=\Delta v+(1-q_\varepsilon(t))v,&x\in D_t,\\
 v=0,&x\in\partial D_t,\\
 v(0,x)=\varepsilon\varphi(x),&x\in D_0.
 \end{cases}
\]
For large $L$, the initial support lies strictly inside $D_0$.
Moreover,
\[
 (\partial_t-\Delta-1+q_\varepsilon)U_\varepsilon
 =(q_\varepsilon-U_\varepsilon)U_\varepsilon\ge0
 \quad\hbox{in }D_t.
\]
Thus $U_\varepsilon\ge v$ by the parabolic comparison principle.
One can apply comparison separately on the two time intervals
on which $q_\varepsilon$ is continuous. On each finite time
interval the solutions are bounded. To justify comparison on
the unbounded domain, add
$\delta\mathrm e^{(2N+2)t}(1+|x|^2)$ to $U_\varepsilon$, apply
comparison on $D_t\cap B_R$ for sufficiently large $R$, and
then let $R\to\infty$ and $\delta\downarrow0$. The added
function has nonnegative residual under
$\partial_t-\Delta-1+q_\varepsilon$ and dominates the bounded
solutions on the artificial outer boundary.

To compute $v$, write
\[
 x=x_\perp+(h+2t-A)\theta,\qquad
 x_\perp\in\theta^\perp,\quad h>0,
\]
and let $\widetilde v(t,x_\perp,h)=v(t,x)$. Then
\[
 \widetilde v_t=\Delta_{x_\perp,h}\widetilde v
       +2\partial_h\widetilde v+(1-q_\varepsilon)\widetilde v.
\]
The substitution
$\widetilde v=\mathrm e^{-h-\Lambda_\varepsilon(t)}Z$
reduces this equation to $Z_t=\Delta Z$ on $h>0$, with zero
Dirichlet boundary value and initial datum
\[
 Z(0,y_\perp,h_0)
 =\varepsilon\mathrm e^{h_0}\varphi(y_\perp+(h_0-A)\theta).
\]
The method of images gives the Dirichlet kernel
\[
 G_t^{N-1}(x_\perp-y_\perp)
 \bigl[G_t^1(h-h_0)-G_t^1(h+h_0)\bigr],
 \qquad
 G_t^d(a)=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\mathrm e^{-|a|^2/(4t)}.
\]
Using
\[
 \frac{G_t^1(h+h_0)}{G_t^1(h-h_0)}=\mathrm e^{-hh_0/t},
 \qquad
 \mathrm e^{h_0-h}G_t^1(h-h_0)
 =\mathrm e^tG_t^1(h-h_0+2t),
\]
we obtain the exact formula
\begin{equation}\label{eq:seed-dirichlet-kernel}
 v(t,x)=\varepsilon\mathrm e^{t-\Lambda_\varepsilon(t)}
 \int_{\mathbb R^N}G_t^N(x-y)
 \left(1-\mathrm e^{-(A+\theta\cdot y)(A+\theta\cdot x-2t)/t}\right)
 \varphi(y)\,\mathrm d y,
 \qquad x\in D_t.
\end{equation}
The integral may be taken over $\mathbb R^N$ because the support of
$\varphi$ lies in $D_0$. This identity follows entirely from
the fixed-half-space heat equation and its explicit kernel.
It also constructs the bounded solution used in the comparison:
the factor in parentheses belongs to $[0,1]$ on the support,
so $0\le v(t,x)\le\varepsilon\mathrm e^t(G_t^N*\varphi)(x)$.
The compact initial support is separated from $\partial D_0$,
which ensures compatibility at the initial boundary; $v$ is
continuous across $t=A/2$ and classical on either side of it.

At $x=(m(T)+\rho\sqrt T)\theta$, $\rho\ge0$, the two heights are
\[
 h_0=A+\theta\cdot y\ge\alpha_LL,\qquad
 h_T=A-k\log T+\rho\sqrt T\ge\rho\sqrt T,
 \qquad
 \alpha_L=1-\zeta-\frac{R_0}{L}>0,
\]
for sufficiently large $L$. Hence the kernel factor satisfies
\[
 1-\mathrm e^{-h_0h_T/T}
 \ge1-\mathrm e^{-\alpha_LL\rho/\sqrt T}
 \ge\frac{\alpha_LL\rho}{\sqrt T}
          \mathrm e^{-\alpha_LL\rho/\sqrt T}.
\]
Here we used the valid inequality
$1-\mathrm e^{-v}=\int_0^v\mathrm e^{-s}\,\mathrm d s\ge v\mathrm e^{-v}$ for $v\ge0$.

Define the normalized field and the directional coefficient by
\[
 W(\log t,\rho,\theta)
 =t^{-1/2}\mathrm e^{\rho\sqrt t}
 U_\varepsilon(t,(m(t)+\rho\sqrt t)\theta),\qquad
 c_\varphi(\theta)=c_N\int_{\mathbb R^N}
              \mathrm e^{\theta\cdot y}\varphi(y)\,\mathrm d y.
\]
For $a=\theta\cdot y$ and $y_\perp=y-a\theta$, completing
squares gives the exact identity
\[
 T^{-1/2}\mathrm e^{\rho\sqrt T}\mathrm e^TG_T^N(x-y)
 =c_N\sqrt T\,\mathrm e^a
 \exp\left[-\frac{(\rho\sqrt T-k\log T-a)^2
                         +|y_\perp|^2}{4T}\right].
\]
Since $|y|\le R_0$ on the support and $\rho\ge0$, it follows that
\[
 T^{-1/2}\mathrm e^{\rho\sqrt T}\varepsilon\mathrm e^T
 \int G_T^N(x-y)\varphi(y)\,\mathrm d y
 \ge\varepsilon\sqrt T\,c_\varphi(\theta)
 \exp\left[-d_L-\frac{\rho^2}{4}
                     -\frac{R_0\rho}{2\sqrt T}\right],
\]
where
\[
 d_L=\frac{(k\log T+R_0)^2+R_0^2}{4T}=o(1).
\]
Combining comparison, \eqref{eq:seed-dirichlet-kernel}, and
\eqref{eq:seed-absorption-loss} therefore yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:seed-at-T}
 W(\log T,\rho,\theta)
 \ge\mathrm e^{-\Lambda_\varepsilon(T)-d_L}
       \varepsilon L\alpha_Lc_\varphi(\theta)
       \rho\mathrm e^{-\rho^2/4-c_L\rho},
 \qquad
 c_L=\frac{\alpha_LL+R_0/2}{\sqrt T}=O(L^{-1}),
\end{equation}
uniformly for $\rho\ge0$ and $\theta\in\mathbb S^{N-1}$.
The prefactor $\mathrm e^{-\Lambda_\varepsilon(T)-d_L}=1-o(1)$ is
independent of $\rho$ and $\theta$.

We next propagate \eqref{eq:seed-at-T} with a multiplicative loss tending to zero. Fix
\[
 0<\sigma<1/4,\qquad 0<\nu<1-2\sigma,
\]
and, for $t\ge T$, set
\[
 \eta_t=t^{\sigma-1/2},\qquad X=\rho-\eta_t>0,
 \qquad b_G(t)=L^{-1}(t/T)^{-\nu},
\]
\[
 F(t,\rho)=X\mathrm e^{-(1/4+b_G(t))X^2}.
\]
We record the residual calculation because the
vanishing multiplicative loss is needed for the
sharp coefficient. Put
\[
 c(t)=\frac14+b_G(t),\qquad
 r=m(t)+\rho\sqrt t,
\]
and use logarithmic-time derivatives. Then
\[
 \partial_\tau b_G=-\nu b_G,\qquad
 \partial_\tau\eta_t=(\sigma-\tfrac12)\eta_t.
\]
For
\[
 F=X\mathrm e^{-c(t)X^2},\qquad X=\rho-\eta_t,
\]
direct differentiation gives
\[
 \frac{F_\rho}{F}=X^{-1}-2cX,\qquad
 \frac{F_{\rho\rho}}{F}=-6c+4c^2X^2,
\]
and hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:seed-residual-exact}
 \frac{(\partial_\tau-L_0-p_{\rm rad}\partial_\rho)F}{F}
 =6b_G-\bigl[(1-\nu)b_G+4b_G^2\bigr]X^2
  -(\sigma\eta_t+p_{\rm rad})(X^{-1}-2cX).
\end{equation}
Here $p_{\rm rad}$ and $L_0$ are as in
\eqref{eq:coefficients}.

For sufficiently large $L$, throughout $t\ge T=L^4$
and $X>0$,
\[
 r>m(t)+t^\sigma>2t,\qquad
 -\frac{k}{\sqrt t}\le p_{\rm rad}<0,\qquad
 0<\sigma\eta_t+p_{\rm rad}\le\sigma\eta_t.
\]
The singular term
$-(\sigma\eta_t+p_{\rm rad})X^{-1}$ is therefore nonpositive.
Also $b_G\le L^{-1}$, so $c(t)$ is uniformly bounded.
Since $\nu<1$, Young's inequality gives
\[
 2c(\sigma\eta_t+p_{\rm rad})X
 \le\frac{1-\nu}{2}b_GX^2
       +C_\nu\frac{\eta_t^2}{b_G}.
\]
It follows from \eqref{eq:seed-residual-exact} that
\[
 \frac{(\partial_\tau-L_0-p_{\rm rad}\partial_\rho)F}{F}
 \le6b_G+C_\nu\frac{\eta_t^2}{b_G}.
\]

In radial and angular coordinates, the normalized
logistic equation is
\[
 \partial_\tau W
 =\left(L_0+p_{\rm rad}\partial_\rho+q_c
          +\frac{t}{r^2}\Delta_\theta\right)W
   -tU_\varepsilon W.
\]
Here $W$ is the normalized field defined above.
The positive angular function $c_\varphi$ is smooth, and
\[
 c_N\mathrm e^{-R_0}\int\varphi
 \le c_\varphi(\theta)\lec_N\mathrm e^{R_0}\int\varphi.
\]
Since
$\Delta_\theta\mathrm e^{\theta\cdot y}
=(|y|^2-(\theta\cdot y)^2-(N-1)\theta\cdot y)
\mathrm e^{\theta\cdot y}$, we also have
\[
 |\Delta_\theta c_\varphi|
 \le [R_0^2+(N-1)R_0]c_\varphi.
\]
Thus the angular error has a bound independent of both
$\theta$ and $\varepsilon$.
Moreover, $q_c\ge0$ and $t/r^2\le C/t$ in the
exterior region under consideration. A common
radial upper datum for the small-seed solutions,
together with \eqref{eq:envelope}, gives
\[
 tU_\varepsilon(t,r\theta)
 \le Ct^{1+\sigma}\mathrm e^{-t^\sigma},
 \qquad r\ge m(t)+t^\sigma,
\]
uniformly in $\varepsilon$.

Consequently, define the trial profile
\[
 \Psi_L(t,\rho,\theta)=c_\varphi(\theta)F(t,\rho).
\]
Its full residual satisfies
\[
 \frac{1}{\Psi_L}
 \left[
 \partial_\tau-L_0-p_{\rm rad}\partial_\rho-q_c
 -\frac{t}{r^2}\Delta_\theta+tU_\varepsilon
 \right]\Psi_L
 \le\mathcal R_L(t),
\]
where
\[
 \mathcal R_L(t)
 =6b_G+C_\nu\frac{\eta_t^2}{b_G}
       +\frac Ct+Ct^{1+\sigma}\mathrm e^{-t^\sigma}.
\]
All constants are independent of $\varepsilon$ and
$t\ge T$, with $\sigma,\nu,\varphi$ fixed.

The loss is integrable in logarithmic time.
Indeed,
\[
 \int_T^\infty b_G(t)\frac{\,\mathrm d t}{t}
 =\frac1{\nu L},
\]
and, since $1-2\sigma-\nu>0$,
\[
 \int_T^\infty
 \frac{\eta_t^2}{b_G(t)}\frac{\,\mathrm d t}{t}
 =\frac{LT^{2\sigma-1}}{1-2\sigma-\nu}
 =\frac{L^{8\sigma-3}}{1-2\sigma-\nu}.
\]
Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:seed-loss}
 \int_T^\infty\mathcal R_L(t)\frac{\,\mathrm d t}{t}
 \le
 \frac6{\nu L}
 +\frac{C_\nu L^{8\sigma-3}}{1-2\sigma-\nu}
 +\frac CT
 +C\int_T^\infty t^\sigma\mathrm e^{-t^\sigma}\,\mathrm d t
 =o(1).
\end{equation}
Since $\sigma<1/4$, we have $8\sigma-3<0$.
Thus the correction factor
\[
 \exp\left[
 -\int_T^t\mathcal R_L(s)\frac{\,\mathrm d s}{s}
 \right]
 =1-o(1)
\]
uniformly for $t\ge T$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$.
Multiplying $\Psi_L$ by this factor makes its
full residual nonpositive.

It remains to fit the initial data.
At $t=T$, write $\rho=X+\eta_T$.
The ratio of
$\rho\mathrm e^{-\rho^2/4-c_L\rho}$ to $F(T,\rho)$
is bounded below, uniformly for $X>0$, by
\[
 \exp\left[
 -\frac{(\eta_T/2+c_L)^2}{4b_G(T)}
 -\frac{\eta_T^2}{4}-c_L\eta_T
 \right]=1-o(1).
\]
Indeed, $b_G(T)=L^{-1}$, $c_L=O(L^{-1})$, and
$\eta_T=L^{4\sigma-2}$ imply
\[
 \frac{(\eta_T/2+c_L)^2}{b_G(T)}
 =O(L^{8\sigma-3}+L^{-1})=o(1),
 \qquad \eta_T^2+c_L\eta_T=o(1).
\]
Thus the full exponential loss in the Dirichlet-kernel lower
bound is compatible with the same initial fitting and does
not change the limiting coefficient.
To track all losses explicitly, put
\[
 D_L=\frac{(\eta_T/2+c_L)^2}{4b_G(T)}
             +\frac{\eta_T^2}{4}+c_L\eta_T,
 \qquad
 E_L=\Lambda_\varepsilon(T)+d_L+D_L
                 +\int_T^\infty\mathcal R_L(s)\frac{\,\mathrm d s}{s}.
\]
For fixed $\zeta,\sigma,\nu,\varphi$, every term is nonnegative
and $E_L=o(1)$, independently of the direction. Define
\[
 \underline W(t,\rho,\theta)
 =\varepsilon L\alpha_L
 \exp\left[-\Lambda_\varepsilon(T)-d_L-D_L
           -\int_T^t\mathcal R_L(s)\frac{\,\mathrm d s}{s}\right]
 c_\varphi(\theta)F(t,\rho).
\]
The initial fitting above gives
$\underline W(T,\rho,\theta)\le W(\log T,\rho,\theta)$
for every $\rho>\eta_T$ and every direction. The residual is
nonpositive, and $\underline W=0$ at $\rho=\eta_t$.

For completeness, comparison on the unbounded moving exterior
can be justified in physical coordinates. Set
\[
 \underline u(t,r\theta)=\sqrt t\,\mathrm e^{-\rho\sqrt t}
                  \underline W(t,\rho,\theta),\qquad
 \rho=\frac{r-m(t)}{\sqrt t},\quad r>m(t)+t^\sigma.
\]
The normalized equation implies
\[
 (\partial_t-\Delta-1+U_\varepsilon)\underline u\le0,
 \qquad
 (\partial_t-\Delta-1+U_\varepsilon)U_\varepsilon=0.
\]
Here $U_\varepsilon$ is a fixed bounded coefficient; this is
linear comparison, not a claim that $\underline u$ solves
the nonlinear logistic equation. On each finite interval
$[T,T_1]$, $\underline u$ tends to zero as $r\to\infty$
uniformly in time and direction, by its Gaussian formula.
For $\delta>0$, the function
$U_\varepsilon+\delta\mathrm e^{t-T}$ is a supersolution of the same
linear equation, since its added term has residual
$\delta\mathrm e^{t-T}U_\varepsilon\ge0$. For a sufficiently large
outer radius it dominates $\underline u$ there; it also
dominates the initial and moving inner-boundary data.
Comparison on the truncated moving annulus, followed by
letting the outer radius tend to infinity and
$\delta\downarrow0$, gives $\underline u\le U_\varepsilon$.
As $T_1$ is arbitrary, this comparison holds for all $t\ge T$.

Now fix $\varepsilon$ and any $\rho>0$, and let $t\to\infty$.
Then $\eta_t,b_G(t)\to0$ and
$F(t,\rho)\to\rho\mathrm e^{-\rho^2/4}$. The homogeneous version of
\eqref{eq:cone-profile}, applied to the fixed datum
$\varepsilon\varphi$, identifies the limit of $W$ as
$a_{\varepsilon,\varphi}(\theta)\rho\mathrm e^{-\rho^2/4}$.
Dividing the comparison by this positive Gaussian profile gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:seed-coefficient-loss}
 a_{\varepsilon,\varphi}(\theta)
 \ge\varepsilon L\alpha_L\mathrm e^{-E_L}c_\varphi(\theta)
 \qquad(\theta\in\mathbb S^{N-1}).
\end{equation}
The right-hand error is independent of $\theta$; no convergence
rate uniform in $\varepsilon$ is needed, because the large-time
limit has already been taken for each fixed $\varepsilon$.
Next let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ with $\zeta$ fixed. Since
$\alpha_L\to1-\zeta$ and $E_L\to0$, the liminf in
\eqref{eq:small-seed} is at least
$-\zeta\sup_\theta c_\varphi(\theta)$. Finally let
$\zeta\downarrow0$. This proves \eqref{eq:small-seed} with the
exact coefficient $c_\varphi$, without requiring any of the
error estimates to be uniform as $\zeta\downarrow0$.

head: environment
name: Small seeds for a general KPP reaction

title: Proof
body_md:
The scaling cancellation used in \cite[Section 7.2]{Wang} applies in every dimension. Choose $C_f\ge1$ such that $f(u)\ge u-C_fu^2$ on $[0,1]$, and let
\[
 (w_\varepsilon)_t
 =\Delta w_\varepsilon+w_\varepsilon-C_fw_\varepsilon^2,
 \qquad
 w_\varepsilon(0)=\varepsilon\varphi,
 \qquad
 \varepsilon\|\varphi\|_\infty\le1/C_f.
\]
If $U_{\varepsilon,f}$ is the homogeneous $f$-solution with the same initial density, comparison gives $w_\varepsilon\le U_{\varepsilon,f}$.

The function $C_fw_\varepsilon$ solves the standard logistic equation with initial density $C_f\varepsilon\varphi$. Lemma~\ref{lem:logistic-seed} therefore yields
\begin{align}\label{eq:cancel}
 a[w_\varepsilon](\theta)
 &=C_f^{-1}a_{\log,C_f\varepsilon\varphi}(\theta)
 \notag\\
 &\ge(1-o(1))\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon)c_N
       \int_{\mathbb R^N}\mathrm e^{\theta\cdot x}\varphi(x)\,\mathrm d x.
\end{align}
Here $a[w_\varepsilon]$ denotes the diffusive leading-edge coefficient. The factor $C_f$ cancels, and replacing $\log(1/(C_f\varepsilon))$ by $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ changes the bound only by a relative $o(1)$.

The homogeneous $f$-amplitude exists by the Cartesian argument of Section~\ref{sec:Cartesian}. Comparison in the diffusive leading edge transfers \eqref{eq:cancel} to that amplitude, uniformly in direction.

label: prop:lower
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Lower coefficient

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $S>0$ and set
\[
 v_S(x)=v(S,x',|x_N|).
\]
For $0<\zeta<1$, choose a nonnegative smooth compactly supported function $\varphi$, even in $x_N$, such that $\varphi\le(1-\zeta)v_S$. The strict margin on its compact support and \eqref{eq:finite-linear} imply that, for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, both folded components at time $S$ dominate $\varepsilon\varphi$.

The homogeneous solution from this even initial density has equal interface traces and zero normal derivative. It therefore satisfies every interface condition. Comparison gives
\[
 a_{1/\varepsilon}(\theta)
 \ge\mathrm e^{-2S}a_{\varepsilon,\varphi}(\theta).
\]
The factor $\mathrm e^{-2S}$ follows from $m(t)-m(t-S)\to2S$ and the normalized leading-edge asymptotics.

The even extension of \eqref{eq:linear-input} has source $2p_\infty\delta_\Sigma$. Its critical mass identity gives
\[
 \mathrm e^{-2S}\int_{\mathbb R^N}\mathrm e^{\theta\cdot x}v_S(x)\,\mathrm d x
 =2\int_0^S\mathrm e^{-2t}\int_\Sigma
       \mathrm e^{\theta'\cdot x'}p_\infty(t,x',0)\,\mathrm d x'\,\mathrm d t.
\]
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:small-seed}, approximate $(1-\zeta)v_S$ from below by such functions $\varphi$, and then let $\zeta\downarrow0$ and $S\to\infty$. The fixed-time Gaussian tails and the exponential input tail on $\Gamma_\delta$ make these passages uniform in direction.

label: lem:early

head: environment
name: Early absorption

label: eq:tilted-gaussian
title: Proof
body_md:
A common compactly supported radial datum $\psi$ and linear heat comparison give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tilted-gaussian}
 V_\varepsilon(t,x):=
 \mathrm e^{-2t+\theta\cdot x}Q_\varepsilon(t,x)
 \le\int_{\mathbb R^N}\mathrm e^{\theta\cdot a}
       G_t^N(x-a-2t\theta)\psi(a)\,\mathrm d a.
\end{equation}
For every $P_0>0$, choose $C_{P_0}$ sufficiently large. Outside
\[
 |x-2t\theta|\le C_{P_0}(t+L),
\]
the integral of $(1+|2t-\theta\cdot x|)V_\varepsilon$ is bounded by $C_{P_0}\mathrm e^{-P_0L}\mathrm e^{-ct}$. Completing the square on a hyperplane gives the corresponding trace estimate.

Fix $\theta\in\Gamma_\delta$ and project onto its
longitudinal coordinate. Write
$Z_\perp\in\theta^\perp$ for the physical transverse
integration variable, with $\,\mathrm d Z_\perp$ denoting
Lebesgue measure on this subspace. Define
\begin{align*}
 \mathfrak f(t,z)
 &=\mathrm e^z\int_{\theta^\perp}
 Q_\varepsilon\bigl(t,(2t+z)\theta+Z_\perp\bigr)
 \,\mathrm d Z_\perp,\\
 \mathfrak b(t,z)
 &=\mathrm e^z\int_{\theta^\perp}
 g\!\left(
 Q_\varepsilon\bigl(t,(2t+z)\theta+Z_\perp\bigr)
 \right)\,\mathrm d Z_\perp\ge0.
\end{align*}
Then
\[
 \int_\mathbb R\mathfrak f(t,z)\,\mathrm d z=M_\varepsilon(t,\theta),
 \qquad
 \int_\mathbb R\mathfrak b(t,z)\,\mathrm d z=B_\varepsilon(t,\theta).
\]
Define the positive source measure by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:projected-source-measure}
 \int_\mathbb R\chi(z)\,
       \mathcal J_{\varepsilon,\theta}(t,\,\mathrm d z)
 =2\varepsilon\mathrm e^{-2t}\int_\Sigma
 \mathrm e^{\theta'\cdot x'}s_\varepsilon(t,x')
 \chi(\theta'\cdot x'-2t)\,\mathrm d x'
\end{equation}
for every bounded Borel function $\chi$. Projecting \eqref{eq:source} yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:projected-heat}
 (\partial_t-\partial_{zz})\mathfrak f
 =-\mathfrak b+\mathcal J_{\varepsilon,\theta},
 \qquad \mathfrak f(0,\cdot)=0,
\end{equation}
in space--time distributions, with source $\,\mathrm d t\,\mathcal J_{\varepsilon,\theta}(t,\,\mathrm d z)$. The critical weight and the shift $\theta\cdot x=2t+z$ cancel linear growth and longitudinal drift; integration over $\theta^\perp$ removes transverse diffusion. Gaussian truncation justifies these operations.

No density of the source in $z$ is required. In particular, for the normal direction,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normal-projected-source}
 \mathcal J_{\varepsilon,e_N}(t,\,\mathrm d z)
 =2\varepsilon j_\varepsilon(t,e_N)\,
       \delta_{-2t}(\,\mathrm d z).
\end{equation}

We also need the absolute input moment
\[
 j_{\mathrm{abs},\varepsilon}(t,\theta)
 =\mathrm e^{-2t}\int_\Sigma
 |\theta'\cdot x'-2t|\mathrm e^{\theta'\cdot x'}
 s_\varepsilon(t,x')\,\mathrm d x'.
\]
Let $d_0>0$ be the distance of the initial support from $\Sigma$. The linear Neumann bound for $p_\infty$ and $s_\varepsilon\le p_\infty$ imply
\begin{equation}\label{eq:absolute-input-bound}
 j_\varepsilon(t,\theta)
 +j_{\mathrm{abs},\varepsilon}(t,\theta)
 \le C(1+t)t^{-1/2}
       \exp[-\delta^2t-d_0^2/(4t)],
 \qquad t>0.
\end{equation}
Indeed, the tilted tangential Gaussian has mean $a'+2t\theta'$ for $a$ in the initial support. The expected absolute centered factor is therefore at most $C(1+t+\sqrt t)\le C'(1+t)$.

It follows that, for every $A\ge0$,
\begin{align}\label{eq:projected-source-bounds}
 \mathcal J_{\varepsilon,\theta}(t,\mathbb R)
 &=2\varepsilon j_\varepsilon(t,\theta),\notag\\
 \int_0^\infty\int_\mathbb R(z+A)_+\,
       \mathcal J_{\varepsilon,\theta}(t,\,\mathrm d z)\,\mathrm d t
 &\le2\varepsilon\left[
 A J_\varepsilon(\theta)
 +\int_0^\infty
       j_{\mathrm{abs},\varepsilon}(t,\theta)\,\mathrm d t
 \right]\notag\\
 &\le C_\delta\varepsilon(A+1),\notag\\
 \int_S^\infty
       \mathcal J_{\varepsilon,\theta}(t,\mathbb R)\,\mathrm d t
 &\le C_\delta\varepsilon\mathrm e^{-c_\delta S},
 \qquad S\ge1.
\end{align}
The total space--time source mass is $2\varepsilon J_\varepsilon=O_\delta(\varepsilon)$. These estimates involve no division by $|\theta'|$ and are therefore uniform up to the normal direction.

Set $A=(1+\gamma_0)L$ and work on $z>-A$. Let $b_A(t)=\mathfrak f(t,-A)$ be the actual wall trace. Using $Q_\varepsilon\le1$ inside the large ball and \eqref{eq:tilted-gaussian} outside it gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:wall}
 b_A(t)\le\overline b_A(t):=
 C\varepsilon^{1+\gamma_0}(t+L)^{N-1}
 +C\mathrm e^{-P_0L}\mathrm e^{-ct}.
\end{equation}
The Dirichlet heat kernel and boundary Poisson kernel on this half-line are
\begin{align*}
 D_A(r;z,\zeta)
 &=G_r^1(z-\zeta)-G_r^1(z+\zeta+2A)\ge0,\\
 P_A(r,z)&=\frac{z+A}{r}G_r^1(z+A)\ge0.
\end{align*}
Discarding the nonpositive absorption term in \eqref{eq:projected-heat} gives
\begin{align}\label{eq:measure-halfline-comparison}
 \mathfrak f(t,z)\le{}&
 \int_0^t\int_{(-A,\infty)}
 D_A(t-s;z,\zeta)
 \mathcal J_{\varepsilon,\theta}(s,\,\mathrm d\zeta)\,\mathrm d s
 \notag\\
 &+\int_0^tP_A(t-s,z)\overline b_A(s)\,\mathrm d s,
 \qquad z>-A.
\end{align}

For completeness, this comparison follows by testing against nonnegative backward Dirichlet heat solutions. The boundary term is the Poisson contribution of the actual trace $b_A$, which is bounded by \eqref{eq:wall}. One may first use positive initial times and finite spatial cutoffs. The Gaussian bound removes the outer cutoff, while \eqref{eq:MB} gives
\[
 0\le M_\varepsilon(s,\theta)
 \le2\varepsilon\int_0^s j_\varepsilon(r,\theta)\,\mathrm d r
 \longrightarrow0
 \qquad(s\downarrow0).
\]
Thus the initial term vanishes. Approximation of nonnegative terminal test functions then gives \eqref{eq:measure-halfline-comparison}, with the kernel integrated directly against the source measure.

Only the source restricted to $(-A,\infty)$ appears in the interior integral. Source at or to the left of the wall affects the half-line through its actual trace, already controlled by \eqref{eq:wall}. For example, the atom in \eqref{eq:normal-projected-source} lies inside the half-line for $s<A/2$ and outside it for $s>A/2$. Its crossing time carries no atom in the time measure.

For $d=\zeta+A>0$, direct integration gives
\begin{align}\label{eq:halfline-kernel-masses}
 \int_{-A}^\infty D_A(r;z,\zeta)\,\mathrm d z
 &=\frac2{\sqrt\pi}
   \int_0^{d/(2\sqrt r)}\mathrm e^{-v^2}\,\mathrm d v
 \le\min\left\{1,\frac d{\sqrt{\pi r}}\right\},
 \notag\\
 \int_{-A}^\infty P_A(r,z)\,\mathrm d z
 &=\frac1{\sqrt{\pi r}}.
\end{align}
Tonelli's theorem applies to these nonnegative integrals, including atomic sources.

Split the source times at $T/2$. By \eqref{eq:projected-source-bounds} and \eqref{eq:halfline-kernel-masses}, the source contribution to the mass at time $T$ is at most
\begin{align*}
 &\frac C{\sqrt T}
 \int_0^{T/2}\int_\mathbb R(\zeta+A)_+\,
       \mathcal J_{\varepsilon,\theta}(s,\,\mathrm d\zeta)\,\mathrm d s
 +\int_{T/2}^T
       \mathcal J_{\varepsilon,\theta}(s,\mathbb R)\,\mathrm d s\\
 &\qquad\le C_\delta\left[
 \frac{\varepsilon(A+1)}{\sqrt T}
 +\varepsilon\mathrm e^{-c_\delta T}\right].
\end{align*}
The wall contribution is bounded by
\[
 \int_0^T
 \frac{\overline b_A(s)}{\sqrt{\pi(T-s)}}\,\mathrm d s
 \le C\left[
 \varepsilon^{1+\gamma_0}\sqrt T(T+L)^{N-1}
 +\mathrm e^{-P_0L}\sqrt T\right].
\]

For the mass with $z\le-A$, use $\mathrm e^zQ_\varepsilon\le\mathrm e^{-A}$ inside the large ball and \eqref{eq:tilted-gaussian} outside it. This gives
\[
 C\varepsilon^{1+\gamma_0}(T+L)^N+C\mathrm e^{-P_0L}.
\]
Adding the three contributions and using $A+1=O(L)$, we obtain
\begin{align}\label{eq:M-T}
 M_\varepsilon(T)\le C\bigl[
 &\varepsilon L/\sqrt T+\varepsilon\mathrm e^{-cT}
 +\varepsilon^{1+\gamma_0}(T+L)^N\notag\\
 &+\varepsilon^{1+\gamma_0}\sqrt T(T+L)^{N-1}
 +\mathrm e^{-P_0L}(1+\sqrt T)\bigr].
\end{align}
With $T=\varepsilon^{-\eta_0}$, the restriction on $\eta_0$ makes the two volume terms $o(\varepsilon)$. The first two terms also have this property, and choosing $P_0>1+\eta_0/2$ controls the last term.

Finally, integrating \eqref{eq:MB} from $T$ to infinity and using $M_\varepsilon(\infty)=0$ gives
\[
 \int_T^\infty B_\varepsilon(t)\,\mathrm d t
 =M_\varepsilon(T)
  +2\varepsilon\int_T^\infty j_\varepsilon(t)\,\mathrm d t
 =o(\varepsilon).
\]
This proves both assertions in \eqref{eq:early}.

label: prop:upper
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Upper coefficient

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $D_x=2t-\theta\cdot x$ and fix $\gamma_0>0$. Choose
\[
 0<\eta_0<
 \min\{1,\gamma_0/[2(N+2)]\},
 \qquad
 T=\varepsilon^{-\eta_0},\qquad
 T_2=\varepsilon^{-4}.
\]
Then $T<T_2$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:early} applies at time $T$.

On $0\le t\le T$, use
\[
 D_x\le A+(D_x-A)_+,\qquad A=(1+\gamma_0)L.
\]
The constant part contributes at most
\[
 A\int_0^TB_\varepsilon(t)\,\mathrm d t
 \le2(1+\gamma_0)\varepsilon L J_\varepsilon.
\]
For the excess, inside $|x-2t\theta|\le C_{P_0}(t+L)$ use
\[
 \mathrm e^{-D_x}g(Q_\varepsilon)\le C_f\mathrm e^{-D_x},
 \qquad
 (D_x-A)_+\mathrm e^{-D_x}\le C\mathrm e^{-A}.
\]
Spatial and time integration gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:early-excess}
 C\varepsilon^{1+\gamma_0}(T+L)^{N+2}
 =o(\varepsilon L).
\end{equation}
Outside the ball, $g(Q_\varepsilon)\le C_fQ_\varepsilon$ and \eqref{eq:tilted-gaussian} give an arbitrarily large exponential power of $\varepsilon$.

On the intermediate interval $T\le t\le T_2$, split at $D_x=C_0L$. The constant part is bounded by
\[
 C_0L\int_T^\infty B_\varepsilon(t)\,\mathrm d t
 =o(\varepsilon L).
\]
The excess is controlled by the same volume argument:
\[
 C\varepsilon^{C_0}(T_2+L)^{N+2}
 +O(\varepsilon^{P_0}).
\]
Choose $C_0>4(N+2)+2$ and then $P_0$ sufficiently large. This contribution is also $o(\varepsilon L)$.

For $t\ge T_2$, choose $\sigma=1/16$ in \eqref{eq:absorption-tail}. The absolute centered absorption is bounded by
\[
 C\int_{T_2}^\infty t^{-11/8}(1+\log t)\,\mathrm d t
 =O(\varepsilon^{3/2}L)
 =o(\varepsilon L).
\]
Finally, \eqref{eq:JK} makes the source first moment in \eqref{eq:amplitude-absorption} $O_\delta(\varepsilon)$. Combining the three time intervals yields
\[
 c_N^{-1}a_{1/\varepsilon}(\theta)
 \le2(1+\gamma_0)\varepsilon L I_N(\theta)
       +o_\delta(\varepsilon L).
\]
For each fixed $\gamma_0$, all error estimates are uniform on $\Gamma_\delta$. Let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and then $\gamma_0\downarrow0$ to conclude.

label: lem:tangential
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Tangential Laplace asymptotics

title: Proof
body_md:
Use polar coordinates on the $(N-1)$-dimensional interface. With $d=N-1$, the angular Laplace formula is
\[
 \int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}\mathrm e^{br\eta\cdot\omega'}
       g(\omega')\,\mathrm d\omega'
 \sim
 \mathrm e^{br}\left(\frac{2\pi}{br}\right)^{(d-1)/2}g(\eta).
\]
For $d=1$, the angular integral is a two-point sum: the forward term gives the displayed expression, while the backward term is exponentially smaller.

For the profiles considered here, the formula can be used uniformly in $\eta$. On compact positive longitudinal intervals, homogeneous leading-edge convergence for $P$ is uniform in direction, and its limiting angular amplitude is continuous. The radial Gaussian envelope controls the remaining longitudinal ranges and supplies an integrable majorant.

First consider $r\le m(t)$. Using $P\le1$ and the angular upper bound gives a contribution
\[
 O\bigl(\mathrm e^{-2\lambda t}t^{-2+k\lambda}\bigr).
\]
For $r>m(t)$, write
\[
 r=m(t)+\rho\sqrt t,\qquad
 P(t,r\omega)=\sqrt t\,\mathrm e^{-\rho\sqrt t}
             w_P(\log t,\rho,\omega).
\]
Combining the angular factor, the radial Jacobian, and $\,\mathrm d r=\sqrt t\,\,\mathrm d\rho$ yields, when $\lambda t\le M$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:trace-main}
 \begin{aligned}
 F_b(t,\eta)
 ={}&\left(\frac{4\pi}{b}\right)^\alpha
       \mathrm e^{-2\lambda t}t^{-1+k\lambda}
       \int_0^\infty\mathrm e^{-\lambda\sqrt t\rho}
       w_P(\log t,\rho,(\eta,0))\,\mathrm d\rho\\
 &+o\bigl(\mathrm e^{-2\lambda t}t^{-1}\bigr).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The error is uniform in $\eta$ and $\lambda t\le M$. To obtain this expression, first restrict $\rho$ to a compact subset of $(0,\infty)$, where $r/(2t)\to1$ uniformly, and then remove the restriction using the Gaussian envelope. The contribution near $\rho=0$ is controlled by the same envelope.

In this regime,
\[
 \lambda\sqrt t\to0,\qquad
 t^{k\lambda}\to1,\qquad b\to1,
\]
uniformly, while
\[
 w_P(\log t,\rho,(\eta,0))
 \longrightarrow
 a_\mathrm{Neu}(\eta,0)\rho\mathrm e^{-\rho^2/4}.
\]
Since
\[
 \int_0^\infty\rho\mathrm e^{-\rho^2/4}\,\mathrm d\rho=2,
\]
dominated convergence in \eqref{eq:trace-main} proves \eqref{eq:tangent-tail}.

For the upper bound, use the angular Gaussian estimate and the radial envelope directly, without imposing $\lambda t\le M$. The factor $\mathrm e^{-\lambda\sqrt t\rho}$ is at most one, and the remaining longitudinal integral is uniformly bounded. Together with the interior estimate, this gives \eqref{eq:tangent-bound}.

body_md:
\label{lem:linear-envelope}
Fix $0\le\sigma<1/2$ and $0<\mu<1/8$, and set
\[
 \eta_t=t^{\sigma-1/2},\qquad
 X=\rho+\eta_t,\qquad a_\mu=1/8+\mu.
\]
There is $T=T(N,\sigma,\mu)\ge2$ and a positive supersolution $\Phi_\tau\ge\mathcal P\Phi$ on $t\ge T$, $\rho\ge-\eta_t$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Phi-bounds}
 c\eta_t\mathrm e^{-a_\mu X^2}
 \le\Phi(\tau,\rho)
 \le C(X+\eta_t)\mathrm e^{-a_\mu X^2}.
\end{equation}
For every radial solution with compactly supported initial density in $[0,1]$ and reaction satisfying \eqref{ass:K}, a constant multiple of $\Phi$ dominates $W$ throughout this domain. The comparison constants may depend on the radial datum and on $N,\sigma,\mu$, but not on the interface resistance.

In physical coordinates, the inner boundary is $z=r-m(t)=-t^\sigma$. In particular, $\sigma=0$ gives $z=-1$. The choices $\mu=1/32$ and $\mu=3/32$ give the Gaussian exponents $5/32$ and $7/32$, respectively.

label: eq:linear-conjugation
title: Proof
body_md:
All coefficients below are evaluated at $\rho=X-\eta_t$. After increasing $T$, we have
\[
 r\ge2t-k\log t-t^\sigma\ge t.
\]
Define
\[
 \ell_1=p_{\rm rad}-\sigma\eta_t,\qquad
 \ell_2=q_c-\tfrac X4\ell_1,\qquad
 \mathcal M=-\partial_{XX}+\tfrac{X^2}{16}-\tfrac34.
\]
For $\Phi=\mathrm e^{-X^2/8}F(\tau,X)$, differentiation at fixed $\rho$, using $\partial_\tau\eta_t=(\sigma-1/2)\eta_t$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:linear-conjugation}
 \mathrm e^{X^2/8}(\partial_\tau-\mathcal P)\Phi
 =\mathcal RF
 :=F_\tau+\mathcal MF-\ell_1F_X-\ell_2F.
\end{equation}
Here $F_\tau$ on the right is taken at fixed $X$.

The coefficient bounds follow from
\begin{align*}
 q_c&=\frac{(N-1)(r-2t)}{2r},
 &|p_{\rm rad}|&\le C_Nt^{-1/2},\\
 |q_c|&\le C_N\left(
 \frac{\log t}{t}+\frac{X+\eta_t}{\sqrt t}\right),
 &|q_c|&\le C_N.
\end{align*}
Consequently, for all $X\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:linear-errors}
 |\ell_1|\le C\eta_t,\qquad
 |\ell_2|\le C\eta_t(1+X),\qquad
 |\ell_2|\le C(1+X).
\end{equation}
These estimates include $\sigma=0$, for which $\ell_1=p_{\rm rad}$ and $\log t/t=O(t^{-1/2})$. The coefficients become small on every fixed $X$-interval. We do not require $\ell_2$ to be uniformly small on the entire half-line.

We now choose the three spatial profiles. Let $\chi\in C^\infty(\mathbb R;[0,1])$ be nonincreasing, equal to one on $(-\infty,0]$ and zero on $[1,\infty)$. For example, take
\[
 E(s)=
 \begin{cases}
 \mathrm e^{-1/s},&s>0,\\
 0,&s\le0,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 \chi(s)=\frac{E(1-s)}{E(s)+E(1-s)}.
\]
Set
\begin{gather*}
 \phi_1(X)=\cos(\pi X),\qquad
 \gamma_1(X)=\chi(12X-3),\qquad
 \gamma_2(X)=1-\chi(X-1),\\
 \varphi_0(X)=X\mathrm e^{-X^2/8},\qquad
 G_\mu(X)=\mathrm e^{-\mu X^2}.
\end{gather*}
Thus $\gamma_1=1$ on $[0,1/4]$ and vanishes on $[1/3,\infty)$, while $\gamma_2=0$ on $[0,1]$ and equals one on $[2,\infty)$. Moreover,
\[
 \phi_1\gamma_1\ge0,\qquad
 -\phi_1''=\pi^2\phi_1,\qquad
 \mathcal M\varphi_0=0.
\]
The positive mode $\varphi_0$ bridges the two cutoff regions.

Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:linear-Phi}
 \Phi=\mathrm e^{-X^2/8}\left[
 \frac{Q(\tau)}2\phi_1(X)\gamma_1(X)
 +\frac{Q(\tau)}2\gamma_2(X)G_\mu(X)
 +\zeta_{\rm lin}(\tau)X\mathrm e^{-X^2/8}
 \right].
\end{equation}
We first estimate its residual under the assumptions
\[
 Q,\zeta_{\rm lin}>0,\qquad Q'\ge-Q,\qquad \zeta_{\rm lin}'\ge0,
\]
where primes denote logarithmic-time derivatives. The coefficient equations chosen below will ensure all three conditions.

For $0\le X\le1/4$, we have $\phi_1\ge2^{-1/2}$ and $|\phi_1'|\le\pi\phi_1$. By \eqref{eq:linear-errors}, increasing $T$ gives
\[
 \pi^2+X^2/16-3/4-|\ell_1|\pi-|\ell_2|\ge1.
\]
Since $\varphi_0$ and $\varphi_0'$ are bounded on this interval, and $\zeta_{\rm lin}'\varphi_0\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:linear-near}
 \mathcal RF\ge
 \left[\tfrac12(Q'+Q)-C_1\zeta_{\rm lin}\eta_t\right]\phi_1.
\end{equation}

For the far region, put $d_\mu=1/16-4\mu^2>0$. Direct calculation gives
\[
 (\mathcal M-\ell_1\partial_X-\ell_2)G_\mu
 =
 \left[d_\mu X^2+2\mu-3/4
       +2\mu\ell_1X-\ell_2\right]G_\mu.
\]
The bracket is bounded below by $d_\mu X^2-C(1+X)$, uniformly for $t\ge T$. Choose $R\ge2$ so that this lower bound is at least one for $X\ge R$. Also, \eqref{eq:linear-errors} and $\mu<1/8$ give
\[
 |\ell_1\varphi_0'+\ell_2\varphi_0|
 \le C\eta_t(1+X^2)\mathrm e^{-X^2/8}
 \le C_2\eta_tG_\mu.
\]
Since $\gamma_1=0$ and $\gamma_2=1$ in this region,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:linear-far}
 \mathcal RF\ge
 \left[\tfrac12(Q'+Q)-C_2\zeta_{\rm lin}\eta_t\right]G_\mu,
 \qquad X\ge R.
\end{equation}

On the remaining compact interval $1/4\le X\le R$, all cutoff profiles and their first two derivatives are bounded, and $\min\varphi_0>0$. Using $Q'\ge-Q$ and \eqref{eq:linear-errors}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:linear-middle}
 \mathcal RF\ge
 \left[\zeta_{\rm lin}'-C_3(Q+\zeta_{\rm lin}\eta_t)\right]\varphi_0.
\end{equation}
Choose $K\ge\max\{2C_1,2C_2,C_3,1\}$ and solve
\begin{equation}\label{eq:linear-odes}
 Q'+Q=K\zeta_{\rm lin}\eta_t,\qquad
 \zeta_{\rm lin}'=K(Q+\zeta_{\rm lin}\eta_t)
\end{equation}
from positive initial values at $\tau_0=\log T$. Positivity is preserved, $Q'\ge-Q$, and $\zeta_{\rm lin}'\ge0$. Thus \eqref{eq:linear-near}--\eqref{eq:linear-middle}, together with \eqref{eq:linear-conjugation}, prove the supersolution inequality. The cutoffs and constants chosen up to this point depend only on $N,\sigma,\mu$.

We next control the time-dependent coefficients. Set $\mathcal V=Q+\zeta_{\rm lin}/K$. Then
\[
 \mathcal V'=(K+1)\zeta_{\rm lin}\eta_t
 \le K(K+1)\eta_t\mathcal V,
 \qquad
 \int_{\tau_0}^\infty\eta_{\mathrm e^s}\,\mathrm d s<\infty.
\]
Gronwall's inequality and monotonicity of $\zeta_{\rm lin}$ imply
\[
 0<\zeta_{\rm lin}(\tau_0)\le\zeta_{\rm lin}(\tau)\le C.
\]
With $\alpha=1/2-\sigma\in(0,1/2]$, variation of constants gives
\[
 Q(\tau)=\mathrm e^{-(\tau-\tau_0)}Q(\tau_0)
 +K\int_{\tau_0}^{\tau}
       \mathrm e^{-(\tau-s)}\zeta_{\rm lin}(s)\mathrm e^{-\alpha s}\,\mathrm d s.
\]
Dividing by $\eta_t=\mathrm e^{-\alpha\tau}$ yields
\[
 c\eta_t\le Q(\tau)\le C\eta_t
 \qquad(\tau\ge\tau_0).
\]
These constants may also depend on the positive initial coefficients.

The near-origin term, the positive mode on compact subintervals of $X>0$, and the far Gaussian term now give \eqref{eq:Phi-bounds}. In particular,
\[
 \Phi(\tau,-\eta_t)=Q(\tau)/2\ge c\eta_t.
\]
The upper bound uses $a_\mu<1/4$, so that the mode $X\mathrm e^{-X^2/4}$ decays faster than the far Gaussian.

It remains to fit the comparison data. Take a compact radial upper datum $U_0\in[0,1]$ as in Section~\ref{sec:prelim}, supported in $\{r\le R_0\}$. At the fixed starting time $T$, linear heat comparison gives
\[
 U(T,r)\le C_T
 \exp\left(-\frac{(r-R_0)_+^2}{4T}\right).
\]
Fix $a_\mu<\nu<1/4$, substitute
\[
 r=m(T)+\sqrt T(X-\eta_T),
\]
and multiply by $T^{-1/2}\mathrm e^{\sqrt T(X-\eta_T)}$. Absorbing the resulting linear term in $X$ into the Gaussian yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:linear-initial}
 W(\tau_0,X-\eta_T)
 \le C_{T,\nu}\mathrm e^{-\nu X^2},
 \qquad X\ge0.
\end{equation}
Because $\nu>a_\mu$, a constant multiple of the lower bound in \eqref{eq:Phi-bounds} dominates this initial field on the entire half-line.

At the moving inner boundary, $U\le1$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:linear-wall}
 W(\tau,-\eta_t)
 \le t^{-1/2}\mathrm e^{-t^\sigma}
 =\eta_t t^{-\sigma}\mathrm e^{-t^\sigma}
 \le\eta_t.
\end{equation}
For $\sigma=0$, the bound is exactly $\mathrm e^{-1}\eta_t$ before the last inequality. Since \eqref{eq:linear-odes} is linear and homogeneous in $(Q,\zeta_{\rm lin})$, multiplying both initial coefficients by one sufficiently large constant fits \eqref{eq:linear-initial} and \eqref{eq:linear-wall}. We continue to denote the rescaled supersolution by $\Phi$.

We finally justify comparison at spatial infinity. On each finite logarithmic-time interval $[\tau_0,\tau_1]$, the heat bound implies that $W\to0$ uniformly as $X\to\infty$. Add
\[
 \varepsilon\mathrm e^{A(\tau-\tau_0)}
\]
to $\Phi$, where $A\ge\sup(1+q_c)$ on the domain. This added function is a supersolution in the original $\rho$ coordinates. For fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and sufficiently large $L$, it dominates $W$ on the outer boundary $X=L$.

Apply comparison on the moving strip $0\le X\le L$, then let $L\to\infty$ and $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. This proves $W\le\Phi$ on $[\tau_0,\tau_1]$. Since $\tau_1$ is arbitrary, the comparison holds for all later times. The interface solutions are first bounded by the common radial solution $U$, so the resulting constants are uniform for $\beta\in[0,\infty]$, including both interface traces.

For $z\ge0$, multiply the upper bound in \eqref{eq:Phi-bounds} by $\sqrt t\,\mathrm e^{-z}$ to obtain
\[
 U(t,m(t)+z)
 \le C(z+2t^\sigma)\mathrm e^{-z}
 \exp\left[
 -a_\mu\left(\frac z{\sqrt t}+\eta_t\right)^2
 \right].
\]
This gives \eqref{eq:envelope}; the choice $\sigma=0$ also gives \eqref{eq:sharp-upper}. The bounded interval $2\le t\le T$ is covered by the compact-data heat bound after increasing the constant. The construction uses neither reaction-specific wave convergence nor concavity.
